## This week’s sociological question

<div class="chapter-question">Where can a model assist an iterative qualitative analysis without replacing the researcher’s engagement with cases, context and counterevidence?</div>

## Connection to the preceding material

Week 2 began with a construct and a predefined label set. Qualitative analysis often begins less settled. Codes develop, comparisons redirect attention and memos connect passages to emerging ideas. The problem is not only whether a model applies a rule correctly, but how its suggestions reorganize the researcher’s attention.

## Learning outcomes

You should be able to distinguish retrieval, coding, theming and interpretation; describe familiarization, focused coding, constant comparison and memo-writing; assign an LLM a bounded role; trace a proposed theme to source passages and negative cases; and explain what a source-complete record still cannot establish.

## Essential readings and what each contributes

::: {.reading-list}
- **Methods:** Timmermans and Tavory (2012), “Theory Construction in Qualitative Research,” *Sociological Theory*. Read the complete article. It explains abductive analysis: surprising observations become analytically useful through comparison with alternative theoretical accounts. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1177/0735275112457914). [@TimmermansTavory2012]
- **Methods and LLMs:** Than et al. (2025), “Updating ‘The Future of Coding’,” *Sociological Methods & Research*. Read the complete article. It provides a researcher–LLM–researcher workflow and an empirical comparison of human and model-assisted coding. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1177/00491241251339188). [@ThanEtAl2025]
- **Substantive application:** Viterna (2006), “Pulled, Pushed, and Persuaded,” *American Journal of Sociology*. Read the complete article. Viterna uses life histories and event-level comparisons to explain different routes into high-risk mobilization; we use it to see what qualitative analysis must preserve before asking an LLM for themes. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1086/502690). [@Viterna2006]
:::

## Additional readings grouped by purpose

- **For reflexivity about the model interaction:** Ibrahim and Voyer (2026), “Qualitative Research with LLM Chatbots,” *Qualitative Research*. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1177/14687941251390794). [@IbrahimVoyer2026]
- **For evidence that suggestions can influence subsequent judgment:** Williams-Ceci et al. (2026), “Biased AI Writing Assistants Shift Users’ Attitudes on Societal Issues,” *Science Advances*. Their experiments concern writing and political attitudes rather than qualitative analysis, but they show why retaining a pre-model interpretation matters. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.adw5578). [@WilliamsCeciEtAl2026]
- **For a recent empirical implementation:** Jack, Cooper and Flower (2026), “Automating the Qualitative Interview?” *Methodological Innovations*. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1177/20597991261448157). [@JackCooperFlower2026]

## Sociological and methodological background

Qualitative analysis is not a single request for “the themes.” Researchers read and re-read material, write provisional codes, compare passages and cases, record hunches, search for exceptions and revise the relationship between data and theory. Timmermans and Tavory emphasize abduction: an unexpected observation becomes productive when it is developed against alternative theoretical accounts. A list of frequent topics is therefore not equivalent to an interpretation.

Viterna shows what this looks like in substantive research. Her explanation of women’s routes into Salvadoran guerrilla organizations depends on reconstructing sequences within life histories and comparing different paths into mobilization. The same broad topic can appear in several accounts while doing different explanatory work. That is exactly the kind of difference a decontextualized list of themes can erase.

Our worked corpus consists of eight instructor-authored fictional excerpts about tenant mutual aid. Each has an ID and text; one also records the interviewer question that shaped the answer. The research question is: **When, if at all, does mutual aid among tenants contribute to political solidarity?** Receiving help alone is not enough: the exercise looks for accounts of tenants identifying a shared problem and acting together. The excerpts include both joint action and clear countercases, so a proposed theme has to survive comparison rather than just sound plausible.

## Synthesis of the current LLM literature

Than and colleagues show that models can contribute useful code suggestions while researchers retain decisions about meaning and iteration. Ibrahim and Voyer ask researchers to document how the chatbot’s categories and conversational affordances enter the analysis. Both point away from one-shot automation. But retaining the final decision does not guarantee an independent judgment. In two preregistered writing experiments, Williams-Ceci and colleagues found that biased AI suggestions shifted participants’ subsequently reported attitudes, usually without participants recognizing the influence. The participants were not qualitative researchers, so this is evidence of a plausible risk rather than a direct test of qualitative analysis. It nevertheless makes the timing of a suggestion methodologically important.

Our workflow therefore begins with a short independent memo. The researcher then makes three visible model calls: request a provisional pattern, reply with a countercase, and ask what evidence supports the proposed explanation. After each reply, they reopen the cited source. The final memo belongs to the researcher. Context windows are large but finite; calls may not preserve cumulative analytic memory; summaries can smooth over contradictions; and a model can cite genuine passages while overstating what they show. Viterna gives us the harder standard: can the analysis preserve chronology, comparison across cases and evidence that does not fit the first proposed theme?

## Summary and preparation for next week

An LLM can widen the set of possible codes or retrieve passages quickly. The analysis still depends on context, comparison, cumulative memo-writing and the researcher’s account of why an interpretation changed. Week 4 asks how the source record itself is produced when the evidence is visual, auditory and sequential.
